title: Johns Hopkins Medicine taps OpenEvidence to bring AI into medical education, clinical care
source_used: Unite.AI (account of the joint OpenEvidence and Johns Hopkins Medicine announcement of 13 Oct 2026)
key_facts: OpenEvidence and Johns Hopkins Medicine announced a strategic collaboration on 13 Oct 2026 to reshape medical education and clinical care for the era of AI.
The announcement rests on two pillars: preparing the next generation of clinicians, and grounding patient care in current evidence-based clinical guidelines.

They plan to design a medical education model that keeps the foundations (pathophysiology, evidence-based medicine, clinical reasoning) and to create adaptive AI systems that help physicians keep learning.
They also plan 'human-first' AI systems for care delivery that combine the best available evidence, the patient's own history and Johns Hopkins best practices.
The announcement calls OpenEvidence the most widely adopted medical AI in the US (a claim by the two organisations).

Quoted: Sanjay Desai, Vice Dean for Education at Johns Hopkins Medicine; Sara Murray, Chief Medical Informatics & AI Officer at Johns Hopkins Medicine; Travis Zack, Chief Medical Officer of OpenEvidence.
Earlier OpenEvidence deals named in the coverage: Penn Medicine (15 Sep 2026, more than 10,000 clinicians), Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (16 Sep 2026), AdventHealth (1 Oct 2026).
No launch dates, costs or results are given; the systems are described as planned.
quote_evidence: The partnership is built on two foundational pillars: readying the next generation of clinicians for the environment in which they will practice, and grounding every patient’s care in the most current evidence-based clinical guidelines.
OpenEvidence and Johns Hopkins Medicine said they will also develop human-first AI systems designed to improve care delivery.
The Johns Hopkins announcement follows several OpenEvidence collaborations with health systems and academic medical centers announced in the preceding weeks.
why_it_matters_hint: Doctors may be trained and supported with an AI evidence tool built into one of the best-known US medical schools and hospital systems, but the plans are aims, not results.
